# Learning goals

In this lab you will:

- use the four functions that R provides for each distribution: `d` (mass or density), `p` (cumulative probability), `q` (quantile) and `r` (random numbers);
- work with the binomial, geometric, Poisson, uniform, normal, exponential and gamma distributions;
- plot pmfs, pdfs and cdfs;
- compute probabilities and quantiles, and check them against hand calculations;
- compare a distribution with real data.

Work in pairs. Plan for 60–75 minutes.

# The naming rule

For a distribution called `xxx`, R has `dxxx`, `pxxx`, `qxxx` and `rxxx`.

| Prefix | Meaning | Discrete $X$ | Continuous $X$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `d` | mass / density | $P(X=x)$ | $f(x)$ |
| `p` | cdf | $P(X\le q)$ | $P(X\le q)$ |
| `q` | quantile | smallest $x$ with $F(x)\ge p$ | $F^{-1}(p)$ |
| `r` | random sample | $n$ draws | $n$ draws |

| Distribution | R name | Parameters in R |
|---|---|---|
| Binomial $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ | `binom` | `size`, `prob` |
| Geometric | `geom` | `prob` |
| Poisson $\mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)$ | `pois` | `lambda` |
| Uniform $U(a,b)$ | `unif` | `min`, `max` |
| Normal $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | `norm` | `mean`, `sd` (not the variance) |
| Exponential $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ | `exp` | `rate` $=\lambda$ |
| Gamma | `gamma` | `shape`, `rate` |

**Warning.** R's geometric counts the *failures before the first success* ($x=0,1,2,\dots$). Many textbooks count the *trial* of the first success ($1,2,\dots$). The two differ by one: if $T$ is the trial number then $P(T=t)=\texttt{dgeom}(t-1,p)$.

# Setup

```{r}
disc   <- read.csv("data/discoveries.csv")    # year, count
rivers <- read.csv("data/rivers.csv")         # length_miles
str(disc); str(rivers)
```

# Binomial

$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(10, 0.3)$: the number of successes in 10 independent trials, each with probability 0.3.

```{r}
dbinom(3, size = 10, prob = 0.3)        # P(X = 3)
choose(10, 3) * 0.3^3 * 0.7^7           # the same by hand
pbinom(3, 10, 0.3)                      # P(X <= 3)
sum(dbinom(0:3, 10, 0.3))               # the same: sum of the pmf
1 - pbinom(3, 10, 0.3)                  # P(X > 3)
pbinom(6, 10, 0.3) - pbinom(2, 10, 0.3) # P(3 <= X <= 6)
qbinom(0.5, 10, 0.3)                    # median
c(mean = 10 * 0.3, var = 10 * 0.3 * 0.7)
```

Plot the pmf and the cdf:

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
x <- 0:10
plot(x, dbinom(x, 10, 0.3), type = "h", lwd = 3, xlab = "x", ylab = "P(X = x)",
     main = "Bin(10, 0.3): pmf")
plot(x, pbinom(x, 10, 0.3), type = "s", xlab = "x", ylab = "P(X <= x)",
     main = "cdf")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Your turn.** A multiple-choice test has 20 questions with 4 options each. A student guesses every answer. (a) Find the probability of exactly 8 right answers. (b) Find the probability of at least 10. (c) What is the smallest score that is reached or exceeded with probability at most 5%? Use `qbinom(0.95, 20, 0.25)` and think about what it returns.

# Geometric

How many failures before the first success when $p=0.2$?

```{r}
dgeom(0:4, 0.2)                 # P(0 failures), ..., P(4 failures)
0.8^3 * 0.2                     # P(3 failures then a success) by hand
pgeom(4, 0.2)                   # P(at most 4 failures) = 1 - 0.8^5
1 - 0.8^5
```

Memorylessness: $P(X\ge 5+3\mid X\ge 5)=P(X\ge 3)$.

```{r}
(1 - pgeom(7, 0.2)) / (1 - pgeom(4, 0.2))
1 - pgeom(2, 0.2)
```

**Your turn.** A die is rolled until the first six. What is the probability that the six appears on the 4th roll or later? Remember that R counts failures, so the first six on roll $t$ means $t-1$ failures.

# Poisson

$X\sim\mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)$ models counts of rare events. The `discoveries` data give the number of great discoveries per year between 1860 and 1959, with mean about 3.1.

```{r}
lambda <- mean(disc$count)
lambda
dpois(0:3, lambda)
ppois(5, lambda)                        # P(X <= 5)
1 - ppois(6, lambda)                    # P(X >= 7)

obs <- table(factor(disc$count, levels = 0:10))
exp_counts <- 100 * dpois(0:10, lambda)
round(rbind(observed = as.numeric(obs), expected = exp_counts), 1)
```

```{r}
barplot(as.numeric(obs) / 100, names.arg = 0:10, col = "grey85",
        xlab = "discoveries in a year", ylab = "relative frequency")
points(seq(0.7, by = 1.2, length.out = 11), dpois(0:10, lambda),
       pch = 19, col = "red", type = "b")
```

The Poisson model describes the data fairly well, although years with 0 discoveries are more frequent than the model predicts (9 observed against about 4.5 expected).

**Your turn.** The Poisson with $\lambda=3$ approximates $\mathrm{Bin}(100, 0.03)$. Compare `dbinom(0:6, 100, 0.03)` with `dpois(0:6, 3)` side by side.

# Uniform and normal

$U\sim U(0,1)$: the density is 1 on $[0,1]$. The normal density is a bell curve.

```{r}
punif(0.3, 0, 1)
punif(2.5, min = 1, max = 4)            # (2.5 - 1) / (4 - 1)
qunif(0.9, 1, 4)

# Normal: heights with mean 170 and sd 8
pnorm(180, mean = 170, sd = 8)          # P(X <= 180)
pnorm(180, 170, 8) - pnorm(160, 170, 8) # P(160 < X < 180)
qnorm(0.975)                            # about 1.96
qnorm(c(0.05, 0.95), 170, 8)            # 5th and 95th percentiles
pnorm((180 - 170) / 8)                  # standardising gives the same answer
```

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
curve(dnorm(x), -4, 4, lwd = 2, ylab = "density", main = "N(0, 1)")
curve(dnorm(x, 1, 2), -4, 6, lwd = 2, col = "blue", add = TRUE)
curve(pnorm(x), -4, 4, lwd = 2, ylab = "F(x)", main = "cdf of N(0, 1)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# The empirical rule
pnorm(1:3) - pnorm(-(1:3))
```

Shading an area under the density:

```{r}
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, ylab = "density")
xs <- x[x <= 1]
polygon(c(xs, rev(xs)), c(dnorm(xs), rep(0, length(xs))), col = "grey80")
text(-1, 0.1, round(pnorm(1), 3))
```

**Your turn.** Exam marks are $N(65, 12^2)$. (a) What proportion of students score above 80? (b) What mark separates the top 10%? (c) Between which two marks (symmetric around 65) do the middle 50% lie?

# Exponential and gamma

$T\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ has $f(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$, mean $1/\lambda$ and $P(T>t)=e^{-\lambda t}$. A call centre receives on average 4 calls per hour, so waiting times between calls have rate $\lambda=4$ per hour.

```{r}
pexp(0.5, rate = 4)                     # P(wait <= 30 min)
1 - exp(-4 * 0.5)                       # by hand
1 - pexp(0.25, 4)                       # P(wait > 15 min)
qexp(0.5, 4)                            # median = log(2) / 4
log(2) / 4
```

The sum of $k$ independent exponential waiting times is gamma with shape $k$. The gamma function has mean `shape / rate` and variance `shape / rate^2`.

```{r}
pgamma(1, shape = 3, rate = 4)          # P(third call arrives within one hour)
1 - ppois(2, 4)                         # the same event: at least 3 calls in an hour
qgamma(c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), shape = 3, rate = 4)

curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1, rate = 1), 0, 10, lwd = 2, ylab = "density")
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 2, rate = 1), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 5, rate = 1), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "red")
legend("topright", legend = paste("shape =", c(1, 2, 5)),
       col = c("black", "blue", "red"), lwd = 2)
```

The agreement `pgamma(1, 3, 4) == 1 - ppois(2, 4)` is the Poisson–gamma link: the third event occurs before time 1 exactly when there are at least 3 events in $[0,1]$.

**Your turn.** The device lifetime is $\mathrm{Exp}$ with mean 500 hours. (a) Find $P(T>800)$. (b) Find the time $t$ such that 90% of devices fail before $t$. (c) Given the device has survived 300 hours, what is $P(T>800\mid T>300)$? Compare it with $P(T>500)$.

# Real data: river lengths

The `rivers` dataset has the lengths of 141 North American rivers. Is a gamma distribution a sensible model?

```{r}
len <- rivers$length_miles
summary(len)
m <- mean(len); v <- var(len)
shape <- m^2 / v; rate <- m / v           # method of moments
c(shape = shape, rate = rate)

hist(len, breaks = 25, freq = FALSE, col = "grey90", border = "white",
     main = "River lengths", xlab = "miles")
curve(dgamma(x, shape, rate), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
curve(dexp(x, 1 / m), add = TRUE, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("gamma", "exponential"), col = c("red", "blue"), lwd = 2)
```

Compare quantiles of the data with those of the fitted gamma:

```{r}
probs <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)
round(rbind(data = quantile(len, probs),
            gamma = qgamma(probs, shape, rate),
            exponential = qexp(probs, 1 / m)))
qqplot(qgamma(ppoints(length(len)), shape, rate), len,
       xlab = "gamma quantiles", ylab = "observed")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
```

**Your turn.** What fraction of the 141 rivers is longer than 1000 miles? Compare with the probability under the fitted gamma, `1 - pgamma(1000, shape, rate)`. Is the model good in the tail?

# Random numbers

The `r` functions simulate from a distribution. A large sample reproduces the distribution:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
z <- rnorm(10000, mean = 170, sd = 8)
c(mean(z), sd(z), mean(z > 180), 1 - pnorm(180, 170, 8))
hist(z, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "grey90", border = "white", main = "")
curve(dnorm(x, 170, 8), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

Next lab (Session 11) uses these functions for simulation.
